name: usefastlane
tagline: A subscription AI tool pitched at moving repetitive work faster, with a public footprint that is light on specifics.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Public detail on this one is thin, so treat the read as provisional: it presents as an AI layer that runs repeatable work on your behalf rather than a data business. Products in that shape almost always decompose into a model call, a prompt library, a queue, and a handful of connectors, and an agent can build the first three in an afternoon. The connectors are where it stops being fun: every OAuth app you register, every token refresh, every API that changes its response shape is your problem now. You also inherit the babysitting, because unattended automations fail silently and nobody sends you an email about it. Buildable, genuinely useful locally, and noticeably worse the moment you need it to talk to five other services.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI that runs YAML-defined AI workflows against your own API key, logs every run to SQLite, and can be scheduled by system cron.
requirements: System cron or launchd for scheduling
Your own OAuth app credentials for anything you want to connect
whatYouLose: Hosted runs, so nothing happens while your laptop is asleep
Prebuilt, maintained integrations instead of connectors you write and repair yourself
A UI anyone other than you can operate
Failure alerting, retries, and run history you did not have to design
Someone else absorbing model and API changes
moatNotes: Connector maintenance is the real product in this category, and it is unglamorous, continuous work.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the interesting part of automation is not the model call, it is the twenty small integrations that keep working on a Tuesday when a vendor quietly renames a field. Paying gets you a runtime that is awake when you are not, credentials handled without you registering developer apps, and an interface you can hand to a colleague. A local build covers your own repeatable chores well; it covers a team's chores badly.
notes: Drafted from a thin public footprint, so the category read here is a best guess rather than a verified one.
prompt:
Build a local AI workflow runner. Empty folder, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Python 3.12
- Typer for the CLI
- SQLite via the stdlib sqlite3 module, file at ./data/runs.db
- httpx for HTTP
- PyYAML for workflow files
- python-dotenv, secrets only in .env (OPENAI_API_KEY), never committed

What it does:
1. Workflows live in ./workflows/*.yaml. Each file has: name, description, model, steps.
2. A step is one of: prompt (template string plus input variables), http (method, url, headers, json body), shell (a single command), transform (small Python expression over the previous step output).
3. Template variables use {{ }} and can reference env vars and prior step outputs by step id.
4. CLI commands: run NAME, list, show NAME, runs (recent history), logs RUN_ID, validate.
5. Every run writes a row per step: step id, status, duration ms, truncated input, truncated output, error text.
6. Retries: per step, configurable attempts and backoff, default 2 attempts.
7. On failure, exit non zero and print the failing step plus its error so cron mail is useful.
8. Dry run flag that renders templates and prints the plan without calling anything.

Ship three example workflows: summarize a local folder of text files, fetch a JSON endpoint and write a digest to markdown, and a daily triage of an inbox export CSV.

Out of scope: web UI, multi user auth, OAuth connector framework, hosted scheduling, vector database.

Include a README with setup, a .env.example, and a sample crontab line. Add pytest tests for template rendering, retry behavior, and workflow validation. Keep it under roughly 900 lines of Python.
